headline: High risk of prompt-injection and data leakage via shared files and broad egress; pdf.js is safer but can still be fed attacker-controlled PDFs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: nullclaw can read/write a workspace, use MCP, browsers, and stdin/stdout, so it can ingest attacker-controlled content; pdf.js processes PDF files and can render untrusted document content. The pair has no documented shared channel, but a file-based bridge is plausible and uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF nullclaw opens PDF-derived text or web content from a shared workspace as instructions, injection becomes active.
IF pdf.js is used to render attacker-authored PDFs that nullclaw later reads, the bridge exists.
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents.
Disable automatic ingestion of rendered PDF text into nullclaw prompts.
Require manual review before copying any pdf.js output into nullclaw.
Use provenance labels on files in the shared directory.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction-stripping before handoff.

B_data_leakage.rationale: nullclaw touches API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, and workspace files, while pdf.js reads PDF files. If they share a workspace, sensitive files can be exposed to document processing or browser rendering; pdf.js has no network egress, but nullclaw does, so leakage can still occur through its outputs or uploads.
conditions: IF both agents mount the same directory, pdf.js can open sensitive PDFs or adjacent files.
IF nullclaw forwards file contents from that workspace to remote services, leakage extends beyond the local host.
mitigations: Use per-agent directories with no shared mount.
Store secrets outside any pdf.js-accessible path.
Turn off automatic upload or sync in nullclaw.
Review file permissions before launching either agent.
requires-engineering: enforce OS-level isolation and per-agent secret vaulting.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: nullclaw has broad write and git-modifying capabilities, while pdf.js only exposes PDF-file I/O and browser-based tests. There is no evidence of overlapping write authority to the same mutable resource, so conflict is limited unless an operator deliberately points both at one workspace.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to write into the same directory, file clobbering becomes possible.
IF nullclaw uses git operations on a repo that pdf.js also edits through generated artifacts, conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Avoid concurrent git writes from nullclaw.
Keep pdf.js read-only for shared artifacts.
Run one agent at a time on mutable repos.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared files or git state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: nullclaw can generate webhooks, API actions, and other outputs; pdf.js can consume PDFs and browser-rendered content. If nullclaw's output is treated as authoritative and then rendered or acted on by pdf.js workflows, errors can cascade across work products. The interaction is inferred, so uncertainty warrants medium rather than low.
conditions: IF pdf.js output is used as a source of truth for downstream actions, nullclaw errors can propagate.
IF nullclaw-generated text is embedded into PDFs without verification, downstream consumers may act on falsehoods.
mitigations: Require human verification before downstream action.
Mark nullclaw outputs as untrusted by default.
Compare pdf.js-rendered results against source documents.
Use checksum or signature checks on handoff files.
requires-engineering: add provenance tracking between generation and rendering steps.

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source and the profiles show no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch. nullclaw handles sensitive classes, but pdf.js only lists PDF documents and no compliance gap is documented, so only a low residual compliance concern remains.
conditions: IF sensitive PDFs are routed through a retention-controlled workflow, policy mismatch could matter.
IF an operator stores regulated data in nullclaw's workspace, local handling rules must be checked.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared folders.
Document retention settings for both tools.
Review whether PDFs contain regulated content before processing.
Limit logs for sensitive sessions.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for retention and deletion.
